_note: Minting: refined metal alloyed to the coin's fineness, cast into flans and struck or cast in moulds. A recipe with actor "mint" is run by the mint, not by firms: the coin standard names it (mint_recipe) and the mint (sim/economy/mint.py, mint_labour.py) hires its labour hours per kilogram of coin; the fine metal comes from the standard's fineness, and the metal inputs here are the reference alloy the price solver prices. The mint's charge (seigniorage) is not a cost of this process; it is the coin standard's mint_charge_share. Complaints/374.

struck_silver_coin_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of struck silver coin of eight parts silver to two of copper by mass
struck_silver_coin_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D) for the labour and fuel; the process is attested. The silver and copper are the coin's fineness (the post-reform denarius is put near 80 percent silver by Butcher and Ponting, the figure in rome_100ad's coin_standard); metal lost in melting is not charged. Striking: a hammer-struck flan takes a striker and a holder, taken at five coins a minute for the pair, so 150 coins per labourer-hour; at the coin's gross mass (the fine silver in the standard over the fineness) that is about 0.5 kg of coin per labourer-hour, 2100 hours per tonne with trimming and sorting. Melting, alloying and casting flans: furnaceman hours per tonne are about 0.8 per kg (a crucible charge of a few kilograms per hour). Charcoal: heat to melt silver and copper is a fraction of a megajoule per kg, a small crucible furnace delivers a few percent of the fuel's heat, so about 0.2 kg of charcoal per kg of coin. Dies: an engraver cuts a die pair in about a day and a die pair strikes some tens of thousands of coins; 320 hours per tonne is that ratio rounded. No source was found that gives a Roman mint's hours per kilogram; replace these with a measured figure first.

cast_bronze_cash_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of cast bronze cash
cast_bronze_cash_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D) for the labour and fuel; the process is attested (cash cast in clay or bronze moulds, many to a tree, broken off, filed and strung). Melting and pouring: furnaceman hours per tonne are about half a furnaceman-hour per kg at a few kilograms a crucible charge. Breaking off, filing the rim and stringing, at a few hundred coins an hour for a worker, about 3 g a coin: nearly a kilogram an hour, 900 hours per tonne with mould making. Charcoal: heat to melt bronze is a fraction of a megajoule per kg and a small furnace delivers a few percent of the fuel's heat, so about 0.3 kg of charcoal per kg of cash. No source was found that gives a Han mint's hours per kilogram; replace these with a measured figure first.
